Thank you for contacting me to share your concerns about granting Trade Promotion Authority or "fast-track" trade negotiating authority for trade agreements. I share your concerns and appreciate hearing from you on this important issue.

I opposed the fast-track bill, which would grant the President power to negotiate and agree to trade agreements, including the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) agreement, and limit the role of Congress in approving trade agreements to a straight up-or-down vote, with no amendments and only limited debate. Because past trade agreements have an unfortunate record of undermining American manufacturers and workers, I believe Congress needs a greater role, not a reduced role, in ensuring trade agreements are in the country's best interest.

Since NAFTA, the United States has lost 50,000 factories and 5 million good, middle class manufacturing jobs. In just the last few years since we passed a free trade agreement with South Korea, our trade deficit with that country has grown by 80 percent. To ensure that future trade agreements work for most workers in America, it's critical that we change how these deals are structured. Unless trade agreements avoid these problems, Congress shouldn't be prevented from amending them.

Because I did not believe the Senate bill took significant steps to restructure trade agreements that would be eligible for "fast-track" procedures, I worked to improve the bill in several key areas.

Trade agreements need to address the rock-bottom wages in other countries so that increased trade doesn't drag down wages and living standards here at home. The minimum wage in TPP countries Vietnam and Mexico are less than a dollar per hour. I proposed that for any trade agreement to be eligible for "fast-track" procedures, countries participating should have to agree to a minimum wage that increases over time to reduce the disparity with U.S. wages. Trade agreements need real labor and environmental standards and those standards need tough enforcement. The trade agreements the U.S. has entered that did include labor standards included very minimal standards, such as forbidding violence against union organizers. But, even though there have been serious violations of these standards, we have brought only one complaint over violations in the last 25 years. In the seven years since it was filed, that complaint has not yet been resolved. I have proposed ways to increase enforcement of labor standards, and called for tougher enforcement measures to be included in the "fast-track" bill. All free trade agreements since NAFTA have allowed foreign companies to sue local, state, and federal governments if they claim our public health, environmental, or other laws cost them money. These cases are decided by international tribunals, by lawyers who rotate between representing companies and deciding cases. That's an outrageous violation of our sovereignty, and a deeply flawed system. I proposed an amendment requiring that for any trade agreement to be eligible for "fast-track" procedures, our environmental, public health, and consumer protection laws must be protected from these practices. I also proposed an amendment to require that trade agreements protect our right to tell Americans where their food comes from, after the World Trade Organization rule that requiring country-of-origin labeling for beef and pork violates international trade law. A number of countries, including China, as well as several countries who are parties to the TPP, have a history of the government manipulating the value of their currency compared to the dollar to make their products cheaper in America and ours more expensive there. That kind of currency manipulation undercuts American businesses and costs American jobs—it can harm American production by a greater margin than the benefits a trade agreement might provide. We should not agree to any trade agreement that doesn't have strict and enforceable rules against currency manipulation, I worked with several Senate colleagues to propose amendments requiring this. You can read more about the specific amendments I offered by clicking here. You can also see my speech on the floor to the Senate here.

Unfortunately, none of the amendments I proposed even received a vote, and on May 21, 2015, the Senate voted to approve fast-track negotiating authority. As you may know, fast-track legislation had been stalled in the House of Representatives. After procedural maneuvers, the fast-track legislation ultimately passed the House and had to be reconsidered and voted on by the Senate. On June 24, 2015, the Senate voted again to approve fast-track authority and the bill is waiting to be signed into law by the President.

Please know I will continue fighting to ensure that America's trade relationships raise Americans' standards of living, support good-paying jobs here at home, and advance the growth of American businesses and workers.

Thank you, again, for sharing your thoughts. I hope you will continue to send me your views and ideas.

All my best,

Jeffrey A. Merkley United States Senator
